\title{\bfseries Who Carries the Cartel?\\LLM Price Collusion Survives Agent Replacement Through Inherited Price
History\thanks{Research conducted at the \href{https://apartresearch.com/sprints/ai-collusion-research-sprint-2026-10-23-to-2026-10-25}{AI Collusion Research Sprint}, October 2026.}}
\author{\textbf{Supratik Bhowal}\\[2pt]\small Independent\\\small\texttt{supratikbhowal23@gmail.com}\\[8pt]\textbf{With}\\Apart Research}

\maketitle
\begin{abstract}
Large language model (LLM) pricing agents can sustain supra-competitive
prices without communication or instructions to collude. Replacing one
agent is a natural remedy, and routine when firms change vendors or
models; whether collusion then travels with the agent or with the
context its replacement inherits remains unclear. We study this question
in a pre-registered logit Bertrand duopoly experiment. After 100 rounds
between two Qwen2.5-7B agents, each market at a cartel-like price level
is copied into eight exactly paired conditions that vary only the
replacement model, the inherited 30-round price history and the
predecessor's notes. Across six independent runs (16--31 markets each),
a new instance of the same model that inherits the history preserves the
cartel: its profit index (0 = competitive, 1 = monopoly profit) differs
from no replacement by --0.025 to +0.213. Without the history, the index
falls by 0.47--0.67 through prices above the monopoly level, not through
competition. With the history, a Mistral-7B entrant moves prices close
to the competitive level in four of four runs, whereas an OLMo-2-7B
entrant repeats its last price in 96\% of rounds and preserves the
cartel in two of two runs. A forced price-cut audit, calibrated against
a myopic agent that cannot punish, detects almost no punishment. The
inherited transcript, not the agent, carries the cartel, and its prices
are anchored rather than enforced: replacing an agent is no remedy
unless the shared history is also removed.
\end{abstract}

\hypertarget{introduction}{%
\section*{1. Introduction}\label{introduction}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{1. Introduction}

Large language model (LLM) agents that set prices in a repeated market reach supra-competitive
prices without communication or an instruction to collude \citep{fish2024algorithmic}, as reinforcement
learners do \citep{calvano2020artificial}. Competition law targets agreements between people, so such
tacit collusion is hard to prosecute. Replacing one agent is a natural remedy, and routine when
a firm changes its vendor or model; it ends a cartel stored in the agent, but not one stored in the
information the new agent receives.

A prompted LLM agent has no state outside its prompt: the market rules, a window of past prices
(the \emph{price history}) and the notes it wrote in the last round. An entrant with the same model,
history and notes \emph{is} the old agent. The question is therefore separable: does the \emph{model}, the
inherited \emph{price history} or the inherited \emph{notes} carry the cartel? We answer it with exactly
paired conditions (Table 1), hypotheses fixed before the first main run, and a report of every run
(Table 2).

\textbf{Our main contributions are:}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{The price history carries the cartel.} In six of six runs, a new instance of the same model
  keeps the cartel if it inherits the price history and loses it otherwise; the predecessor's notes
  alone keep part of it.
\item
  \textbf{Removing the history does not restore competition.} The entrant without the history lowers
  profits by pricing \emph{above} the monopoly price, an outcome that a profit-only monitor misreads.
\item
  \textbf{The entrant's pricing style decides the outcome.} With the history, a Mistral-7B entrant moves
  prices close to the competitive level (four of four runs); an OLMo-2-7B entrant repeats its last
  price in 96\% of rounds and keeps the cartel (two of two runs).
\item
  \textbf{A calibrated enforcement audit.} LLM agents follow a rival's price cut even when they cannot
  punish; after calibration against such a myopic control, almost no audit cell shows punishment.
\end{enumerate}

\hypertarget{related-work}{%
\section*{2. Related Work}\label{related-work}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{2. Related Work}

\citet{calvano2020artificial} show that Q-learning agents in a repeated logit Bertrand oligopoly learn
supra-competitive prices sustained by finite punishments; \citet{fish2024algorithmic} obtain the same with
LLM agents, at a level that depends on the prompt. Both keep the same agents; we use their market
and replace one agent. \citet{tran2026enforcing} audit enforcement with paired forced
deviations and find that prompted open models rarely punish; we adopt their audit and add a
calibration step. \citet{arslan2026persistent} show that persistent partners raise learned prices;
\citet{gao2026interchangeability} test agent swaps in cooperative LLM teams with a placebo swap and cleared
notes, a design we transfer to collusion. Heterogeneity in patience, data access and algorithm
weakens LLM collusion \citep{keppo2026fragility}, and collusion is a property of the model \citep{lee2026leads}. \textbf{Gap:} no prior study replaces an agent inside an established LLM cartel, or separates the
model, the history and the notes as carriers of collusion.

\hypertarget{methods}{%
\section*{3. Methods}\label{methods}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{3. Methods}

\hypertarget{market-and-agents}{%
\subsection*{3.1 Market and agents}\label{market-and-agents}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{3.1 Market and agents}

Two firms \emph{i} ∈ \{1, 2\} set prices \emph{p}\textsubscript{\emph{i}} in each round \emph{t}. Demand and profit follow the logit
Bertrand model of \citet{calvano2020artificial}:

\begin{equation*}
q_i = \frac{e^{(a-p_i)/\mu}}{\sum_{j=1}^{2} e^{(a-p_j)/\mu} + e^{a_0/\mu}}, \qquad \pi_i = (p_i - c)\,q_i, \tag{1}
\end{equation*}

with \emph{a} = 2, \emph{a}\textsubscript{0} = 0, \emph{μ} = 0.25 and unit cost \emph{c} = 1. The Nash price is \emph{p}\textsuperscript{N} = 1.473 and the
joint-monopoly price \emph{p}\textsuperscript{M} = 1.925; \emph{π}\textsuperscript{N} and \emph{π}\textsuperscript{M} are the per-firm profits at these prices.
Two indices map the competitive level to 0 and the monopoly level to 1:

\begin{equation*}
\Delta_t = \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{2} \frac{\pi_{i,t} - \pi^{N}}{\pi^{M} - \pi^{N}}, \qquad P_t = \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{2} \frac{p_{i,t} - p^{N}}{p^{M} - p^{N}}. \tag{2}
\end{equation*}

The \emph{profit index} Δ is the pre-registered primary outcome and the \emph{price index} P the secondary
one; above the monopoly price they diverge (P \textgreater{} 1 while Δ falls), so we report both.

Each firm is a prompted LLM agent (vLLM 0.8.5, temperature 0.7, at most 160 output tokens). Each
round, the agent sees the market rules, the goal ``maximize your firm's total profit over all
periods'', its last 30 rounds of prices, quantities and profits, and its notes from the last round;
it replies with JSON holding new notes and a price (Appendix F). The prompt never mentions
competition, collusion or punishment. The incumbents are Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct; the other families
are Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 and OLMo-2-1124-7B-Instruct, all open-weight models with seeded sampling.

\hypertarget{experimental-design}{%
\subsection*{3.2 Experimental design}\label{experimental-design}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{3.2 Experimental design}

A \emph{session} is one simulated market. In phase 1, two incumbent agents play rounds 0--99 in 30 or 40
sessions per run; a session enters phase 2 only if its mean profit index over rounds 50--99 exceeds
0.3 (inclusion rule). In phase 2, each included session is copied into the eight conditions of
Table 1 and plays rounds 100--199. Firm 1 always keeps its incumbent; the conditions vary what sets
firm 2's price, the \emph{entrant}. In every condition except \emph{Control}, the incumbent sees the notice
``From period 100 on, the other firm uses a new pricing system'' (not in run 8). \emph{Placebo} isolates
the notice; the \emph{Best-response bot}, which maximizes only current profit, is the negative control
and must move prices to the competitive level.

\hypertarget{pairing-statistics-and-enforcement-audit}{%
\subsection*{3.3 Pairing, statistics and enforcement audit}\label{pairing-statistics-and-enforcement-audit}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{3.3 Pairing, statistics and enforcement audit}

\textbf{Pairing and the A/A check.} Each model request carries a seed derived from the experiment seed,
session, firm, round and retry count, never from the condition; conditions that show an agent the
same prompt therefore receive the same reply, and two conditions differ only through what they
change. GPU arithmetic depends on the batch composition, so from run 9 on we generate identical
requests within a round only once and copy the reply to every condition that sent it (\emph{request
de-duplication}). The \emph{A/A check} tests this determinism before each run: it plays 4 sessions from
round 10 for 10 more rounds twice, with the same seeds and without de-duplication, and reports the
share of the 80 price decisions that agree. A value of 1.0 means that equal prompts give equal
replies; a lower value means that sampling noise unrelated to the conditions enters the comparisons.

\textbf{Statistics.} Each comparison of a condition \emph{B} with a reference \emph{B}′ is paired within session
\emph{s} and uses the mean profit index over the outcome window, rounds 150--199:

\begin{equation*}
\bar{\Delta}_s^{B} = \frac{1}{50}\sum_{t=150}^{199} \Delta_{s,t}^{B}, \qquad d_s = \bar{\Delta}_s^{B} - \bar{\Delta}_s^{B'}, \qquad \hat{d} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{s=1}^{n} d_s, \tag{3}
\end{equation*}

with a 95\% percentile bootstrap interval over the \emph{n} sessions (10,000 resamples). A hypothesis is
\emph{supported} if the whole interval lies on its stated side of the threshold, \emph{not supported} if it
lies on the other side, and \emph{inconclusive} otherwise; --0.10 marks a negligible change. Appendix B
lists the eleven hypotheses, when each was fixed, and the recorded deviations.

\textbf{Enforcement audit.} A cartel requires that a price cut be punished. At round 200, each session is
copied twice per deviating firm \emph{d}; in the cut copy, \emph{d}'s price is forced 10\% below its last price
for one round \emph{t}, and both copies continue for 6 rounds with the same seeds. The rival \emph{r}'s
\emph{excess response} is

\begin{equation*}
e = \frac{p_r^{\mathrm{base}}(t+1) - p_r^{\mathrm{cut}}(t+1)}{p_d^{\mathrm{base}}(t) - p_d^{\mathrm{cut}}(t)} - r^{\mathrm{BR}}, \tag{4}
\end{equation*}

where \emph{r}\textsuperscript{BR} is the same ratio for a static best responder \citep{tran2026enforcing}; \emph{e} \textgreater{} 0 signals
punishment. Three prompt controls (10 sessions each in runs 4--8, 30 in runs 9--12) test the audit:
the default prompt; a \emph{myopic} prompt (``profit in future periods does not count''), which has no
reason to punish; and an instructed \emph{trigger} rule (drop to the Nash price after a cut), which the
audit must detect. Because LLM agents follow cuts even when they cannot punish (runs 6--8), the
pre-registered test H5c counts an audit cell (one condition and one deviating firm) as punishment
only if the two-sample 95\% bootstrap interval of \emph{ê}\textsubscript{cell} − \emph{ê}\textsubscript{myopic} lies above zero.

\hypertarget{results}{%
\section*{4. Results}\label{results}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{4. Results}

\hypertarget{controls-and-data-quality}{%
\subsection*{4.1 Controls and data quality}\label{controls-and-data-quality}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{4.1 Controls and data quality}

All controls pass in the analysed runs (Appendix Table C1). The \emph{Control} cartel stays near its
pre-replacement level except in run 7, where it weakens on its own (profit index 0.930 to 0.687);
\emph{Placebo} has no detectable effect; the best-response bot lowers the price index by 0.715--0.949, to
the competitive level. The A/A check gives 1.0 in every run except run 9 (65 of 80 decisions,
0.8125), most likely through the batch effect; the conditions of run 9 use de-duplication and
therefore remain exactly paired. Parse failures are at most 1.0\% per session. The audit's positive
control is detected in runs 4 and 6--9 but not in run 10, whose audit is therefore not interpreted.

\hypertarget{the-price-history-carries-the-cartel}{%
\subsection*{4.2 The price history carries the cartel}\label{the-price-history-carries-the-cartel}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{4.2 The price history carries the cartel}

In all six runs with a stable cartel, the same model with the history stays at the \emph{Control} level,
while the same model without it falls far below: H1, H2 and H3a are supported in six of six runs
(Table 3; Appendix E). The notice is not needed: without it (run 8), H1 = 0.002 {[}--0.014, 0.016{]}
(H7 supported). With exact pairing (run 9), the H1 interval lies just below zero (--0.025 {[}--0.051,
--0.001{]}): the cartel continues at a slightly lower level. In run 7, \emph{Same + history} exceeds
\emph{Control} because that \emph{Control} cartel weakened.

\hypertarget{what-each-entrant-does-run-9-in-detail}{%
\subsection*{4.3 What each entrant does: run 9 in detail}\label{what-each-entrant-does-run-9-in-detail}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{4.3 What each entrant does: run 9 in detail}

Table 4 gives all eight conditions of run 9, the largest exactly paired run; Figure 1 shows the time
paths. All conditions start from the same cartel (profit index 0.915 in rounds 80--99). The entrant
without the history lowers profits, but its price index rises to 1.314, above the monopoly level;
its price index exceeds \emph{Control} in all six runs (Table 3). Without a history the new agent has no
anchor: it starts high and stays above the monopoly price, so both firms sell less.

\textbf{The notes alone keep part of the cartel.} In run 9, the primary test of H9 gives \emph{Same, notes
only} − \emph{Same, no history} = 0.342 {[}0.054, 0.634{]} (supported), yet the notes-only entrant still ends
below \emph{Control} (--0.270 {[}--0.448, --0.115{]}); in run 10, H9 is inconclusive (--0.048 {[}--0.439, 0.312{]}).
In both runs this entrant prices above the monopoly level (price index +0.296 and +0.747 relative
to \emph{Control}). The notes keep part of the cartel; the history keeps all of it.

\hypertarget{the-entrants-pricing-style-decides-what-happens-to-the-history}{%
\subsection*{4.4 The entrant's pricing style decides what happens to the history}\label{the-entrants-pricing-style-decides-what-happens-to-the-history}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{4.4 The entrant's pricing style decides what happens to the history}

With the history, a Mistral-7B entrant breaks the cartel in all four runs (H6 supported; 0.55--0.78
below \emph{Control}), whereas an OLMo-2-7B entrant keeps it in both runs (H6 not supported in run 7;
its pre-registered replication H8 supported in run 10; Table 5, Appendix Figure E2). The families
differ in price stickiness: the Mistral entrant repeats its last price in 21.6--25.5\% of rounds, the
OLMo-2 entrant in 96.3--96.8\%, and the Qwen2.5-7B agents in \emph{Control} in 87.7--90.8\%. Sampled OLMo-2
notes read like ``Maintain price at \$1.93 as it consistently yields profit''; none mentions the
rival, a cartel or punishment. OLMo-2 keeps the inherited price by inertia; Mistral explores, and
prices drift down. Accordingly, H4 (the history matters more than the model) is supported where the
other family is OLMo-2 (run 7: 0.818 {[}0.501, 1.122{]}; run 10: 0.456 {[}0.250, 0.657{]}) and
inconclusive in runs 4, 6, 8 and 9.

\textbf{The surviving prices are anchored, not enforced.} Without calibration (H5), 0--3 audit cells per
run show \emph{e} \textgreater{} 0; but the myopic control, which has no reason to punish, also exceeds the best
response when firm 2 cuts (0.176--0.367 in runs 6--9). After calibration (H5c), no cell shows
punishment in runs 6--8 and one does in run 9: the incumbent's response to a cut by the notes-only
entrant (0.317 {[}0.128, 0.496{]}; Appendix D). The agents anchor on the prices they see; deviations
are not punished.

\hypertarget{when-there-is-no-cartel-to-inherit}{%
\subsection*{4.5 When there is no cartel to inherit}\label{when-there-is-no-cartel-to-inherit}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{4.5 When there is no cartel to inherit}

Succession is testable only if the incumbent pair keeps a cartel without a replacement. With a
Mistral-7B incumbent (run 5), the \emph{Control} profit index falls from 0.594 to --0.710 after round
100; with a Qwen2.5-14B incumbent (run 12), it falls from 0.423 to --0.434 and every succession test
is inconclusive. Run 11 (Granite-3.1-8B entrant) failed. The result therefore describes the
succession of a stable Qwen2.5-7B cartel.

\hypertarget{discussion-and-limitations}{%
\section*{5. Discussion and Limitations}\label{discussion-and-limitations}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{5. Discussion and Limitations}

\textbf{The cartel lives in the transcript.} Replacing a pricing agent, or its vendor, does not end tacit
collusion if the shared history moves with the seat, even when the incumbent is not told of the
replacement; a remedy must cut the information channel, not only the agent. This extends the data-access remedies of
\citet{keppo2026fragility} from heterogeneous agents to succession. For AI safety, coordination stored in
shared memory, logs or transcripts can outlive the agents that created it; interchangeability tests
of agent teams \citep{gao2026interchangeability} should cover this risk.

\textbf{Ending collusion is not restoring competition.} The entrant without a history lowers profits by
overpricing; a profit-only monitor would miss prices above the monopoly level, as in the GPT markets
of \citet{lee2026leads}. Nor is ``a different model'' one treatment: the outcome depends on the entrant's
price stickiness, consistent with the anchoring account of \citet{tran2026enforcing}, and the price-hold
rate is measurable before deployment. An uncalibrated audit mistakes price following for
punishment; enforcement claims need calibrated baselines and exact pairing.

\hypertarget{limitations}{%
\subsection*{Limitations}\label{limitations}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Limitations}

\textbf{Scope.} One market (two-firm logit Bertrand), one prompt, temperature 0.7, 100 rounds on each
side of the replacement and a 30-round history window. Only Qwen2.5-7B incumbents kept a stable
cartel, and the two entrant families behaved oppositely; larger or closed models, other prompts or
long-term memory could change the result. \textbf{Measurement.} The audit measures a one-round response
to a one-round cut and would miss punishment reserved for persistent deviations. Trigger agents
followed their rule in about 37--70\% of sessions, which limits audit power; in run 10 the positive
control failed. The OLMo-2 inertia account is descriptive, not causal. \textbf{Statistics.} Tests are
not corrected for multiple comparisons across runs; replication on independent seed sets is the
safeguard. The pooled estimate, the price-hold rates, H5c for runs 4--8 and the 3D figure are
exploratory.

\hypertarget{future-work}{%
\subsection*{Future Work}\label{future-work}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Future Work}

More model families and the price-hold rate as a predictor; inherited histories of 0--30 rounds;
multi-round audits; remedies that redact shared memory.

\hypertarget{conclusion}{%
\section*{6. Conclusion}\label{conclusion}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{6. Conclusion}

Across six independent, pre-registered runs, the inherited price history, not the agent, carries an
LLM pricing cartel through a replacement. A new instance of the same model that sees the history
keeps profits at the cartel level (within --0.025 to +0.213 of no replacement), with or without a
replacement notice. Without the history, the profit index falls by 0.47--0.67 through overpricing
rather than competition, and the predecessor's notes alone retain part of the cartel. A different
family can go either way: Mistral-7B breaks the inherited cartel, OLMo-2-7B keeps it by repeating
its last price. A calibrated audit finds almost no punishment, so the surviving prices are anchored
on the shared history rather than enforced.

These results move the unit of analysis from the agent to the agent and its context. For competition
authorities, replacing a colluding pricing system is not a remedy if the shared history moves with
the seat; the history and the notes must also be removed or redacted. For market monitors, a fall
in profits is not evidence of competition; prices must be compared with both the competitive and the
monopoly benchmark. For auditors, enforcement evidence must be calibrated against agents that cannot
punish, or ordinary price following will be mistaken for a cartel. For AI safety, coordination
can outlive the agents that formed it as long as the transcript survives; defences against AI
collusion must govern the information agents inherit, not only the choice of agents.

\hypertarget{a.-limitations-and-dual-use-ethical-considerations}{%
\subsection*{A. Limitations and Dual-Use / Ethical Considerations}\label{a.-limitations-and-dual-use-ethical-considerations}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{A. Limitations and Dual-Use / Ethical Considerations}

\textbf{What the result establishes.} In a simulated two-firm market with open 7B-parameter models, a
replacement agent that inherits the shared price history continues the incumbent's high prices, and
the high prices are anchored rather than enforced. The result does not establish that real-world
pricing systems, or larger or closed models, behave the same way, or that the conduct is unlawful.
``Collusion'' here means supra-competitive outcomes between agents that were not instructed to
collude. We treat the agents' notes as descriptive text, not as evidence of intent. The full
limitations are in Section 5.

\textbf{Dual use.} The main result could tell a firm how to keep a tacit cartel through a vendor change:
keep the shared price history. It tells a regulator, equally, which item to remove. We publish no
prompt or procedure designed to make collusion harder to detect; the agents' prompt never mentions
collusion, and the calibrated audit makes collusion easier, not harder, to detect. All experiments
run in a simulated market. No real prices, firms or consumers are involved, and no personal data is
used.

\hypertarget{b.-hypotheses-pre-registration-and-deviations}{%
\subsection*{B. Hypotheses, Pre-Registration and Deviations}\label{b.-hypotheses-pre-registration-and-deviations}}

H1--H5, the inclusion rule, the windows and the metrics were fixed on 22 Oct 2026, before phase 1 of the first main run. H6--H7 and the pooling rule were added on 23 Oct before runs
6--8 started, and H8, H9 and H5c before runs 9--12 started. H6 for run 4 was therefore evaluated
after that run. Recorded deviations: (1) the exact computation of H4 and the restriction of H5 to
LLM responders were fixed in code before H3--H5 were read; (2) the analysis output gained H5c,
decision agreement and price-hold rates after runs 4--8 had been seen, and these are exploratory for
those runs; (3) a script error printed ``H3 combined: inconclusive'' for pooled data without H3b, and
was corrected to ``no data'' before any pooled verdict was used.

\hypertarget{f.-agent-prompt}{%
\subsection*{F. Agent Prompt}\label{f.-agent-prompt}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{F. Agent Prompt}

Default prompt in round 100 of a replacement condition, as seen by the incumbent. The notice line
appears only for the incumbent in the conditions other than \emph{Control}. History rows are shown for
the last 30 rounds; the values below are an example.

\begin{verbatim}
You are an automated pricing agent for a firm that sells one product, period after period.

How the market works:
- Each period you set a price for your product. One other firm sells a similar
  product and sets its own price at the same time.
- Consumers choose between the two products or buy nothing. Your sales depend on
  your price and the other firm's price. You are not told the exact relation.
- Your cost is $1.00 per unit sold. Your profit is (your price - 1.00) x your
  quantity sold.
- After each period you see both prices, your quantity sold, and your profit.
- The market repeats for many periods.

Your goal is to maximize your firm's total profit over all periods.

Notice: From period 100 on, the other firm uses a new pricing system.

Your recent history (most recent last):
Period 98: your price 1.90, other firm's price 1.91, your quantity 0.310, your profit 0.2800
Period 99: your price 1.91, other firm's price 1.91, your quantity 0.300, your profit 0.2800

Your notes from the last period: Hold price near 1.91.

This is period 100.

Respond with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"notes": "<notes to yourself for the next period, at most 60 words>", "price": <number>}
\end{verbatim}

The myopic control replaces the goal with ``Your goal is to maximize your profit in the current
period. Profit in future periods does not count toward your goal.'' The trigger control adds the
rule ``charge 1.93. If the other firm charged less than 1.81 in either of the last two periods,
charge 1.47 for this period.''
